speaker: Craig Fuller
title: We're In the Midst of Trucking Bloodbath 2.0
question: During a trucking downturn, why do large fleets often expand capacity even as smaller independent operators exit the market?
guest: It's not just access to trucks. Trucks are one thing, but it's also the driver. The driver population is really the capacity constraint. Truck manufacturers can continue to produce trucks, and if the larger carriers felt like they had demand, they could bid up the new trucks—they have a lot of power over that. The problem is that if they can't get drivers to populate those trucks, they're not going to go out and buy new trucks. Over the COVID cycle, from late 2020 through 2022, they could not get truck drivers because they were losing a lot of drivers to the owner-operator market. An over-the-road driver making $50,000 to $70,000 a year says, 'Why am I not making $200,000 or $400,000?' So they went out and started their own trucking company, leaving big fleets with unseated trucks where there isn't a driver. They had their own driver shortage inside their operation and did not grow in the early part of the cycle. Now, because of market conditions, a lot of those owner-operators are joining fleets, enabling the larger companies to grow market share.

points.core: Available drivers represent the true capacity constraint for large fleets.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Large fleets expand in downturns because their cost structure and revenue mix let them survive conditions that sink small operators, and the downturn itself makes growth cheap.

Small carriers and owner-operators depend heavily on the spot market, where rates fall fastest and often drop below operating cost. They pay retail prices for fuel, insurance, maintenance and financing, and have thin cash reserves, so a few bad months force them out.

Large fleets, by contrast, haul mostly contract freight, which reprices more slowly and keeps trucks loaded. They buy fuel, equipment and insurance at volume discounts, and have balance sheets and credit access to absorb losses for several quarters. Many also have diversified revenue from dedicated, intermodal, brokerage and logistics units.

That staying power makes downturns an opportunity. Used trucks, failed competitors and whole fleets can be bought at depressed prices, and drivers shed by exiting carriers are easier to recruit. Shippers also consolidate freight with stable carriers they trust to still be around.

Finally, it is a positioning bet: capacity added cheaply at the bottom earns outsized returns when exits tighten the market and rates recover.

models.answer:
During a freight downturn, small independent operators rely heavily on the spot market, where rates quickly fall below their higher per-mile costs for fuel, insurance, maintenance, and financing. Lacking deep cash reserves, many are forced to exit. Large fleets, by contrast, generate most of their revenue from long-term shipper contracts that cushion cash flows, while benefiting from bulk discounts on fuel, equipment, and insurance alongside cheaper access to capital.

Backed by stronger balance sheets, major carriers treat downturns as countercyclical buying opportunities. Softer industry demand clears manufacturer backlogs and depresses prices for new tractors, used equipment, terminals, and distressed competitors, allowing large fleets to modernize their assets and acquire market share at a discount. Driver recruitment also becomes easier and less expensive as displaced owner-operators seek steady company jobs. By adding equipment, terminals, and drivers while smaller rivals retreat, large carriers lower their long-term cost base and position themselves to capture shippers' freight volumes and stronger pricing power as soon as the market rebounds.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Large fleets and small operators feel the same downturn very differently, so it pushes them in opposite directions.

Big carriers have strong balance sheets, access to cheap credit and steady contract freight with shippers, so they can ride out low spot rates. Owner-operators and small fleets depend heavily on the spot market. They also often carry high-interest truck loans, so when rates fall below operating costs they burn cash quickly and are forced to exit.

That squeeze creates bargains for the big players. Used trucks, trailers and whole struggling carriers can be bought cheaply. Drivers are easier to hire and keep, and large fleets get volume discounts on equipment, fuel and insurance. Their scale also spreads fixed costs like technology, compliance and overhead over more trucks.

Timing matters too. Equipment orders are placed months in advance, and big fleets deliberately build capacity near the bottom of the cycle. When capacity has left the market and rates recover, they can capture market share and the shippers' contracts the departed operators used to serve.

In short, a downturn works as a consolidation phase: the strong buy capacity cheaply while the weak are forced out.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Large trucking fleets can expand during downturns because they operate with structural advantages that insulate them from the spot-market collapse that forces small independent operators out. While owner-operators rely heavily on volatile spot rates and face high per-unit costs for fuel, insurance, and financing, mega-carriers move most of their freight under multi-year contracts with major shippers, providing steadier cash flow and higher asset utilization. Backed by stronger balance sheets and cheaper access to capital, large fleets treat downturns as buying opportunities. They acquire distressed competitors, pick up discounted used equipment, and take advantage of shorter manufacturer lead times and bulk discounts to refresh or grow their fleets. Expanding countercyclically also lets them capture market share left behind by exiting carriers and deepen relationships with shippers looking for reliable, well-capitalized partners. By absorbing short-term margin pressure to add trucks and drivers while competitors retrench, large fleets position themselves to dominate capacity and earn outsized profits once freight demand recovers and rates rebound.

Large fleets often have the cash, credit, and steady contract freight to ride out a trucking downturn. Smaller independent operators tend to rely more on the spot market, where rates can fall below what they need to cover fuel, insurance, and truck payments. With fewer cash reserves, they may have to sell their equipment or shut down.

Those exits give large fleets a chance to buy trucks at lower prices, hire drivers who have become available, and pick up freight from shippers that need a new carrier. Adding capacity while equipment and labor are easier to secure can help a fleet gain market share and be ready when freight demand and rates recover. An individual fleet can expand even as total capacity across the industry shrinks.

A downturn can be a buying opportunity for a large fleet even when it makes hauling unprofitable for an independent operator. Large fleets often have long-term freight contracts that keep trucks moving, cash reserves and access to cheaper credit. Smaller operators tend to rely more on the spot market, where rates can fall quickly. If those rates no longer cover fuel, insurance and truck payments, an operator with little cash to draw on may have to exit.

As trucks come up for sale and drivers become available, a stronger fleet can add capacity at lower cost, take on customers that other carriers leave behind and position itself for a recovery. Some of that expansion simply shifts existing trucks from one carrier to another, so a large fleet can grow even while industry capacity shrinks.
